name: Kenneth Kaunda International Airport
before:
Zambia's main airport, in Chongwe District off the Great East Road about 27 km north east of central Lusaka. It carries 71 per cent of all passenger traffic in the country and is the hub for Zambia Airways, Proflight Zambia, Royal Zambian Airlines and Mahogany Air.

The terminal to know is Terminal Two, which opened in August 2021 with six gates and handles every international flight. Terminal One is domestic only and has no jet bridges. The new building came out of a 360 million dollar expansion begun in 2015, with 22 check in counters and twelve border channels.

Transfers are simple. It is a 15 to 20 minute taxi ride into the centre, most Lusaka hotels run their own shuttles, and Avis and Europcar both have desks. There is a bus to Chelston bus station but it does not keep to a timetable.

The airport opened in 1967 and was renamed in 2011 after Kenneth Kaunda, Zambia's first president.
after:
Zambia's main airport, about 27 km north east of central Lusaka. In 2025 it handled more than 70 per cent of the passengers at Zambia's airports, and it is the base for Zambia Airways and Proflight Zambia.

International flights use Terminal Two, which opened in August 2021 as part of a 360 million dollar expansion, and domestic flights use Terminal One.

Taxis are the usual way into the city, and hotels can arrange shuttles. Avis and Europcar offer car hire.

The airport opened in 1967 and was renamed in 2011 after Kenneth Kaunda, Zambia's first president.

claims.claim: in 2025 more than 70 per cent of the passengers at Zambia's airports
claims.inAfter: In 2025 it handled more than 70 per cent of the passengers at Zambia's airports
claims.note: Was 'It carries 71 per cent of all passenger traffic in the country'. The operator's 2025 annual report gives 71 per cent as the airport's share of ENPLANED (paying) passengers; its share of all passengers was 73.57 per cent (1,795,801 of 2,441,100). Wikipedia calls the 71 per cent all passenger traffic. 'More than 70 per cent' is true on both measures, so the text uses that and names the year.

claims.claim: in Chongwe District off the Great East Road
claims.wasBefore: in Chongwe District off the Great East Road
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's airport, transport and contact pages give only the distance from the city (27 km) and a Lusaka post box; the distance and direction are kept.

claims.claim: 71 per cent of all passenger traffic in the country
claims.wasBefore: It carries 71 per cent of all passenger traffic in the country
claims.why: Corrected (see above): 71 per cent is the operator's figure for enplaned passengers in 2025; for all passengers it was 73.57 per cent.

claims.claim: hub for Zambia Airways, Proflight Zambia, Royal Zambian Airlines and Mahogany Air
claims.wasBefore: is the hub for Zambia Airways, Proflight Zambia, Royal Zambian Airlines and Mahogany Air
claims.why: Zambia Airways and Proflight kept as based here. Royal Zambian Airlines and Mahogany Air could not be confirmed as current: neither is among the 15 scheduled airlines in the operator's 2025 annual report, and the operator's airline directory lists only Royal Air Charters, a charter operator. Their own sites could not be found without a search engine.

claims.claim: the terminal to know is Terminal Two, six gates, every international flight
claims.wasBefore: The terminal to know is Terminal Two, which opened in August 2021 with six gates and handles every international flight.
claims.why: Reworded: Terminal Two for international flights and its August 2021 opening are kept. The six gates are cut: the operator's 2023 report gives six aerobridges for the airport as a whole and does not say which terminal has them, so only Wikipedia places them.

claims.claim: Terminal One domestic only, no jet bridges
claims.wasBefore: Terminal One is domestic only and has no jet bridges.
claims.why: Domestic use kept with the operator's April 2026 release. 'No jet bridges' rests on Wikipedia alone.

claims.claim: expansion begun in 2015, 22 check-in counters, twelve border channels
claims.wasBefore: The new building came out of a 360 million dollar expansion begun in 2015, with 22 check in counters and twelve border channels.
claims.why: The 360 million dollar project is kept (operator's 2017 and 2021 reports). The 2015 start and the counter and border-channel numbers rest on Wikipedia alone, quoting the 2015 plans; Lusaka Times, which Wikipedia cites, answered with a Cloudflare check, and the operator's 2016 report is a scanned image with no text.

claims.claim: Transfers are simple
claims.why: A judgement that rested on the 15 to 20 minute taxi time, which is cut.

claims.claim: 15 to 20 minute taxi ride into the centre
claims.wasBefore: It is a 15 to 20 minute taxi ride into the centre
claims.why: Wikipedia alone (citing an unofficial airport guide site). The operator puts the airport 27 km from the business district, which makes 15 to 20 minutes doubtful. Softened to taxis being the usual way in.

claims.claim: most Lusaka hotels run their own shuttles; Avis and Europcar desks
claims.wasBefore: most Lusaka hotels run their own shuttles, and Avis and Europcar both have desks
claims.why: Softened to what both sources say: hotels can arrange shuttles, and Avis and Europcar offer car hire.

claims.claim: bus to Chelston bus station, no timetable
claims.wasBefore: There is a bus to Chelston bus station but it does not keep to a timetable.
claims.why: Sources disagree: Wikipedia describes an irregular bus to Chelston, while the operator's FAQ says 'We currently do not have any public bus services to/from the airport' (the FAQ is undated and partly out of date). Cut rather than choose.

claims.claim: Held back: about 1.8 million passengers in 2025
claims.why: Held back: a verified 2025 passenger total that replaces nothing in the old text (which gave only a share). 1,795,801 passengers in 2025: 1,462,144 international and 333,657 domestic (operator's 2025 annual report; the same figure is in Wikipedia's infobox).

sources.quote: stat1_data = 1,795,801

claims.claim: Held back: FCDO on visas and the KAZA UNIVISA at Lusaka
claims.why: Held back: replaces nothing in the old text. The FCDO (updated 1 June 2026, still current 24 September 2026) says British passport holders do not need a visa for Zambia, that the KAZA UNIVISA (50 US dollars, 30 days, Zambia and Zimbabwe plus day trips to Botswana) can be bought on arrival at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport, and that the 25 US dollar international departure tax is normally in the ticket. Would go in as an attributed statement.

sources.org: UK FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office)
quote: British passport holders do not need a visa to enter Zambia.
It costs 50 US dollars and is valid for 30 days.
On leaving Zambia, all air passengers must pay the equivalent to 25 US dollars for international travel

sources.org: UK FCDO (Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office)
